teaching_documents.title: Carbon reservoirs, transfers and climate connections
source_sections: Effects of Changing the Carbon Cycle
teaching_documents.content: Carbon is stored in rocks, ocean water, the atmosphere, living organisms, soils and fossil fuels. Transfers connect these reservoirs over different timescales. Weathering, sediment formation and tectonic processes belong to the slow geological cycle. Plants and phytoplankton draw carbon dioxide from their surroundings during photosynthesis, using sunlight to build organic matter. Respiration, decomposition and combustion return carbon to the atmosphere. Burning fossil fuels moves previously stored carbon into the active cycle. Carbon dioxide absorbs and re-emits infrared energy, influencing Earth’s energy balance. Some additional atmospheric carbon dissolves in ocean water and changes its chemistry toward greater acidity. A reservoir model distinguishes stored quantities from transfer rates; changing one transfer can affect multiple reservoirs.

teaching_documents.title: Water storage, movement and human effects
teaching_documents.content: The water cycle connects atmospheric, surface and underground stores. Water occurs as liquid, ice and vapor. A pool describes where water is stored; a flux describes its movement between pools. Evaporation changes liquid to vapor, while transpiration releases water from plants. Condensation produces liquid droplets from vapor, and precipitation transfers water to the surface. Runoff carries water across land; infiltration and percolation move it into soil and groundwater. Energy absorption supports evaporation, and gravity helps drive falling precipitation and downhill flow. People alter storage and movement through dams, river diversions and water withdrawals. Water quality also determines whether available water can support people and ecosystems. Describing only a circular evaporation–rain diagram misses these connected pathways and human influences.

teaching_documents.title: Reef ecosystems, biodiversity and coastal services
teaching_documents.content: Coral reefs provide habitat for diverse marine organisms and support food webs and fisheries. Their benefits extend beyond the organisms living directly on a reef: coastal communities obtain food, livelihoods and recreation from reef-associated systems. Reef structure also reduces wave energy reaching shorelines, helping limit erosion and storm damage. Damage to that structure can therefore change risks for nearby communities. Reef organisms participate in processes such as filtering water and forming beach sand. These connections illustrate ecosystem services, where ecological functions benefit people. Conservation decisions can consider habitat condition together with fisheries, shoreline protection and community needs. A reef example supports discussion of interacting species and ecosystem change, but does not represent every terrestrial or freshwater ecosystem.

teaching_documents.title: Resource conservation and the recycling system
teaching_documents.content: EPA’s materials-management hierarchy gives priority to avoiding waste and reusing materials before recycling them. Recycling collects discarded materials and processes them into inputs for manufacturing new products. This can reduce demand for extracting timber, water and minerals, conserve energy and divert material from disposal. Collection alone does not complete the recycling loop: sorting and processing, manufacturing, and purchasing recycled-content products are also involved. A product marked recyclable is not necessarily made with recycled content, and acceptance differs among local collection programs. Practical comparisons should consider material type, collection rules, processing capability and markets for recovered materials. Resource-management solutions involve tradeoffs; reducing unnecessary consumption and keeping useful materials in service can avoid impacts before waste is created.
